title: By train to Brașov
goal: Buy tickets and ask questions at the station, and use object pronouns (*mă, te, îl, o…*) with the marker *pe* — Romanian's way of flagging that the person on the receiving end is a person.
bekal: put object pronouns before the verb: *te aștept*, *îl cunosc*, *o văd*
mark a person object with *pe* and double it with a pronoun: *Îl cunosc pe Andrei. O aștept pe Ioana.*
conjugate *a merge*, *a veni*, *a pleca*, and name transport with *cu* + definite article: *cu trenul*, *cu metroul*, *pe jos*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — La Gara de Nord
dialogs.intro: Friday afternoon at the office, Ioana invites Budi on a trip to Brașov. On Saturday morning Budi is already standing at the ticket window at Gara de Nord.

notes: **Îl cunoști pe Andrei? — Andrei is mentioned twice.** Once through the pronoun *îl* before the verb, and again by name with the marker *pe*. To English ears this sounds redundant ("him you know Andrei?"), but to a Romanian a sentence without *îl* sounds lame. In the answer the pronoun alone is enough: *Da, îl cunosc.*

**Te aștept, vă aștept, ne așteaptă, o văd.** Object pronouns always stand **before** the verb — the opposite of "I'm waiting for *you*", "I see *her*". *Vă aștept pe amândoi*: *amândoi* = "you both" (for two women: *amândouă*), and since they are people, it also gets *pe*.

**Vii și tu?** For "come along" Romanian uses *a veni* (come): *Vii și tu?* — "are you coming?", *Sigur că vin!* — "of course I'm coming!". *A merge* is used when you just name the destination: *Merg la Brașov.*

**La ce oră…? De la ce peron…?** A preposition is never left at the end, as in English "which platform from?"; it always stands before the question word. *Peron* is where passengers stand, *linie* is the track — on station boards and announcements you'll see *linia 5* more often than *peronul 5*. Both are understood.

**Trenul de nouă și jumătate.** *De* + a time turns the time into a label: "the half past nine train". *Are întârziere* (literally "has a delay") and its opposite *la timp* (on time) are the two phrases you'll hear most at the station.

grammars.title: Accusative object pronouns and the marker pe
body: In unit 8 you used *mă, te, se* for actions that come back to yourself. Object pronouns look almost the same — the difference is that they point at someone else: *mă aștepți* = "you're waiting for me". The only truly new ones are in the third person: **îl, o, îi, le**.

If the object is **a specific person** (a name, a relative, a pronoun), it gets the marker **pe**, and the pronoun still appears before the verb. This doubling is what makes a Romanian sentence sound Romanian.

head: Person
Pronoun
Example
Meaning
rows: I'll wait for you at the station.

after: **Things don't take *pe*:** *Aștept trenul. Cumpăr un bilet.* But once the thing has been mentioned, the pronoun is used alone and follows the word's gender: *Ai biletul? — Da, îl am.* · *Bei cafeaua? — Da, o beau.* Neuter words take *îl* in the singular and *le* in the plural.

**The golden rule of unit 6 still applies after *pe*:** a bare noun loses its article — *Îl aștept pe profesor* — but one with a modifier keeps it: *O aștept pe colega mea. Îi cunosc pe părinții tăi.* To ask: *Pe cine aștepți?* — "Who are you waiting for?" (no pronoun here).

**With *nu* and *să*** the pronoun still sits right before the verb: *Nu te văd. Vreau să te ajut.* In speech *îl* and *o* usually merge: *nu-l cunosc*, *n-o văd*, *să-l aștept*, *s-o aștept*; the full forms *nu îl*, *nu o* are also correct.
*O* has one quirk: in the past tense it moves **after** the verb (*am văzut-o*). That comes in unit 15; for now, in the present, everything goes in front.

grammars.title: A merge, a veni, a pleca — and cu + transport
body: Three verbs of motion that split the work neatly: *a merge* = go, head for a destination; *a veni* = come, toward the person you're talking to (or along with them); *a pleca* = leave, depart from a place.
after: **Pleacă, așteaptă:** before the ending *-ă*, the *e* sound breaks into *ea* — *plec, pleci, **pleacă***; *aștept, aștepți, **așteaptă***. The third-person subjunctive (unit 11) goes back to *e*: *să plece, să aștepte*; and *să meargă, să vină*.

**The prepositions:** *merg **la** Brașov* (destination) · *plec **din** București* (from inside a city or room) · *trenul pleacă **de la** linia cinci, vin **de la** birou* (from a point). The partner verb is *a ajunge* (arrive): *Plecăm la nouă și jumătate și ajungem la Brașov la douăsprezece.*

**Transport = *cu* + definite article.** This is the exception to the golden rule mentioned in unit 6: after *cu* the article stays — *cu trenul, cu autobuzul, cu metroul, cu mașina*. The only one without *cu*: **pe jos** — on foot.
*A merge* is also used for things that "run": *Liftul nu merge* — "the elevator is out of order". And *Merge!* alone means "OK, works for me!"

items: *Acesta este trenul de Brașov?* — Is this the train to Brașov?
*La ce oră ajunge trenul la Brașov?* — What time does the train get to Brașov?
*Trebuie să schimb trenul?* — Do I have to change trains?
*Locul acesta este liber?* — Is this seat free?
*Trenul are o întârziere de douăzeci de minute.* — The train is twenty minutes late.

blocks.text: *Dus* means "gone" and *întors* "returned" — *dus-întors* is literally "there-and-back". *Mersul trenurilor* (literally "the running of the trains") contains a plural genitive that comes in unit 13; for now just memorize it whole as the heading on the timetable board.

blocks.title: Taking the train in Romania
items: State passenger trains are run by **CFR Călători**. The two types you'll meet most: **Regio (R)** — cheap, stopping at every small station — and **InterRegio (IR)** — faster, with the *vagon* and *loc* numbers printed on the ticket.

**Gara de Nord** is Bucharest's main station. The line to Brașov climbs the Prahova valley past Sinaia — the mountain town that is home to Peleș Castle — and the trip takes about two and a half to three hours.
Delays are nothing unusual, so get used to glancing at the *întârziere* column on the *plecări* board. The upside: the view of the Carpathians from the window makes an extra half hour fly by.

sections.title: Transport: how do you get there?

items: *Cum mergi la birou? — Merg cu metroul.* — How do you get to the office? — By metro.
*Autobuzul vine în cinci minute.* — The bus is coming in five minutes.
*Doamna Popescu merge la piață pe jos.* — Mrs. Popescu walks to the market.
*Te aștept în stația de metrou.* — I'll wait for you at the metro station.
*Andrei pleacă la Cluj cu avionul; îl aștept pe fratele lui la gară.* — Andrei is flying to Cluj; I'm waiting for his brother at the station.

blocks.title: Getting around Bucharest
items: *Metroul* is the fastest way across the city; buses, trams, and trolleybuses fill in above ground. *Stație* is used for stops and metro stations, while *gară* is only for train stations.

On buses and trams, your ticket or card must be **validated** in the little machine as soon as you board — *a valida biletul*. Inspectors (*controlor*) turn up often, and "I didn't know" won't save you from a fine.
